{{Short description|Type of statistical analysis}}
'''Nonparametric statistics''' is a type of statistical analysis that makes minimal assumptions about the underlying [[Distribution (mathematics)|distribution]] of the data being studied. Often these models are infinite-dimensional, rather than finite dimensional, as in [[parametric statistics]].<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2006 |title=All of Nonparametric Statistics |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/0-387-30623-4 |journal=Springer Texts in Statistics |language=en |doi=10.1007/0-387-30623-4|isbn=978-0-387-25145-5 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Nonparametric statistics can be used for [[descriptive statistics]] or [[statistical inference]]. Nonparametric tests are often used when the assumptions of parametric tests are evidently violated.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Pearce|first1=J|last2=Derrick|first2=B|title= Preliminary testing: The devil of statistics?|journal= Reinvention: An International Journal of Undergraduate Research |date=2019|volume=12|issue=2|doi=10.31273/reinvention.v12i2.339|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Definitions==

The term "nonparametric statistics" has been defined imprecisely in the following two ways, among others:

The first meaning of ''nonparametric'' involves techniques that do not rely on data belonging to any particular parametric family of probability distributions. These include, among others:
* Methods which are ''distribution-free'', which do not rely on assumptions that the data are drawn from a given parametric family of [[probability distributions]]. 
* Statistics defined to be a function on a sample, without dependency on a [[parameter]]. 
An example is [[order statistic]]s, which are based on [[Ranking#Ordinal ranking ("1234" ranking)|ordinal ranking]] of observations.

The discussion following is taken from ''Kendall's Advanced Theory of Statistics''.<ref>Stuart A., Ord J.K, Arnold S. (1999), ''Kendall's Advanced Theory of Statistics: Volume 2A—Classical Inference and the Linear Model'', sixth edition, §20.2–20.3 ([[Edward Arnold (publisher)|Arnold]]).</ref>

<blockquote>
Statistical hypotheses concern the behavior of observable random variables... For example, the hypothesis (a) that a normal distribution has a specified mean and variance is statistical; so is the hypothesis (b) that it has a given mean but unspecified variance; so is the hypothesis (c) that a distribution is of normal form with both mean and variance unspecified; finally, so is the hypothesis (d) that two unspecified continuous distributions are identical.

It will have been noticed that in the examples (a) and (b) the distribution underlying the observations was taken to be of a certain form (the normal) and the hypothesis was concerned entirely with the value of one or both of its parameters. Such a hypothesis, for obvious reasons, is called ''parametric''.

Hypothesis (c) was of a different nature, as no parameter values are specified in the statement of the hypothesis; we might reasonably call such a hypothesis ''nonparametric''. Hypothesis (d) is also nonparametric but, in addition, it does not even specify the underlying form of the distribution and may now be reasonably termed ''distribution-free''. Notwithstanding these distinctions, the statistical literature now commonly applies the label "nonparametric" to test procedures that we have just termed "distribution-free", thereby losing a useful classification.
</blockquote>

The second meaning of ''nonparametric'' involves techniques that do not assume that the ''structure'' of a model is fixed.  Typically, the model grows in size to accommodate the complexity of the data. In these techniques, individual variables ''are'' typically assumed to belong to parametric distributions, and assumptions about the types of associations among variables are also made. These techniques include, among others:
* ''[[nonparametric regression]]'', which is modeling whereby the structure of the relationship between variables is treated nonparametrically, but where nevertheless there may be parametric assumptions about the distribution of model residuals.
* ''nonparametric hierarchical Bayesian models'', such as models based on the [[Dirichlet process]], which allow the number of [[latent variables]] to grow as necessary to fit the data, but where individual variables still follow parametric distributions and even the process controlling the rate of growth of latent variables follows a parametric distribution.

==Applications and purpose==
Nonparametric methods are widely used for studying populations that have a ranked order (such as movie reviews receiving one to five "stars"). The use of nonparametric methods may be necessary when data have a [[ranking]] but no clear [[Number|numerical]] interpretation, such as when assessing [[preferences]]. In terms of [[level of measurement|levels of measurement]], nonparametric methods result in [[ordinal data]].

As nonparametric methods make fewer assumptions, their applicability is much more general than the corresponding parametric methods. In particular, they may be applied in situations where less is known about the application in question. Also, due to the reliance on fewer assumptions, nonparametric methods are more [[Robust statistics#Introduction|robust]].

Nonparametric methods are sometimes considered simpler to use and more robust than parametric methods, even when the assumptions of [[Parametric statistics|parametric methods]] are justified. This is due to their more general nature, which may make them less susceptible to misuse and misunderstanding. Nonparametric methods can be considered a conservative choice, as they will work even when their assumptions are not met, whereas parametric methods can produce misleading results when their assumptions are violated.

The wider applicability and increased [[Robust statistics|robustness]] of nonparametric tests comes at a cost: in cases where a parametric test's assumptions are met, nonparametric tests have less [[statistical power]]. In other words, a larger sample size can be required to draw conclusions with the same degree of confidence.

==Nonparametric models==
''Nonparametric models'' differ from [[parametric statistics|parametric]] models in that the model structure is not specified ''à priori'' but is instead determined from data. The term ''nonparametric'' is not meant to imply that such models completely lack parameters but that the number and nature of the parameters are flexible and not fixed in advance.
* [[Histogram]]: a simple nonparametric estimate of a probability distribution.
* [[Kernel density estimation]]: method to estimate a probability distribution, often based on local averaging.
* [[Smoothing spline|Smoothing splines]]: regression method based on [[Spline (mathematics)|splines]].
* [[Data envelopment analysis]]: provides efficiency coefficients similar to those obtained by [[multivariate analysis]] without any distributional assumption.
* [[k-nearest neighbors algorithm|k-nearest neighbors (kNN)]]: classifies the unseen instance based on the k points in the training set which are nearest to it.
* [[Support vector machine]] (with a Gaussian kernel): a nonparametric large-margin classifier.
* [[method of moments (statistics)|Method of moments]]: estimator for a single value, such as the [[mean]] or the [[variance]] of a distribution.

==Nonparametric tests==
'''Nonparametric''' (or '''distribution-free''') '''inferential statistical methods''' are mathematical procedures for statistical hypothesis testing which, unlike [[parametric statistics]], make no assumptions about the [[probability distribution]]s of the variables being assessed. The most frequently used tests include
* [[Analysis of similarities]]
* [[Anderson–Darling test]]: tests whether a sample is drawn from a given distribution
* [[Bootstrapping (statistics)|Statistical bootstrap methods]]: estimates the accuracy/sampling distribution of a statistic
* [[Chi-squared test]]
* [[Cochran's Q test|Cochran's Q]]: tests whether ''k'' treatments in randomized block designs with 0/1 outcomes have identical effects
* [[Cohen's kappa]]: measures inter-rater agreement for categorical items
* [[Friedman test|Friedman two-way analysis of variance (Repeated Measures)]] by ranks: tests whether ''k'' treatments in randomized block designs have identical effects
* [[Empirical likelihood]]
* [[Kaplan–Meier estimator|Kaplan–Meier]]: estimates the survival function from lifetime data, modeling censoring
* [[Kendall tau rank correlation coefficient|Kendall's tau]]: measures statistical dependence between two variables
* [[Kendall's W]]: a measure between 0 and 1 of inter-rater agreement.
* [[Kolmogorov–Smirnov test]]: tests whether a sample is drawn from a given distribution, or whether two samples are drawn from the same distribution.
* [[Kruskal–Wallis one-way analysis of variance]] by ranks: tests whether >&nbsp;2 independent samples are drawn from the same distribution.
* [[Kuiper's test]]: tests whether a sample is drawn from a given distribution, sensitive to cyclic variations such as day of the week.
* [[Logrank test]]: compares survival distributions of two right-skewed, censored samples.
* [[Mann–Whitney U]] or Wilcoxon rank sum test: tests whether two samples are drawn from the same distribution, as compared to a given alternative hypothesis.
* [[McNemar's test]]: tests whether, in 2 × 2 contingency tables with a dichotomous trait and matched pairs of subjects, row and column marginal frequencies are equal.
* [[Median test]]: tests whether two samples are drawn from distributions with equal medians.
* [[Pitman permutation test|Pitman's permutation test]]: a statistical significance test that yields exact ''p'' values by examining all possible rearrangements of labels.
* [[Rank product]]s: detects differentially expressed genes in replicated microarray experiments.
* [[Siegel–Tukey test]]: tests for differences in scale between two groups.
* [[Sign test]]: tests whether matched pair samples are drawn from distributions with equal medians.
* [[Spearman's rank correlation coefficient]]: measures statistical dependence between two variables using a monotonic function.
* [[Squared ranks test]]: tests equality of variances in two or more samples.
* [[Tukey–Duckworth test]]: tests equality of two distributions by using ranks.
* [[Wald–Wolfowitz runs test]]: tests whether the elements of a sequence are mutually independent/random.
* [[Wilcoxon signed-rank test]]: tests whether matched pair samples are drawn from populations with different mean ranks.
* Universal Linear Fit Identification: A Method Independent of Data, Outliers and Noise Distribution Model and Free of Missing or Removed Data Imputation.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Adikaram |first1=K. K. L. B. |last2=Hussein |first2=M. A. |last3=Effenberger |first3=M. |last4=Becker |first4=T. |title=Universal Linear Fit Identification: A Method Independent of Data, Outliers and Noise Distribution Model and Free of Missing or Removed Data Imputation |journal=PLOS ONE |date=16 November 2015 |volume=10 |issue=11 |article-number=e0141486 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0141486 |doi-access=free |pmid=26571035 |pmc=4646355 |bibcode=2015PLoSO..1041486A |language=en |issn=1932-6203}}</ref>

== Mathematical Statistics ==
In [[mathematical statistics]], nonparametric models are considered models that do not rely on a parametric assumption of the unknown data distribution (in [[density estimation]] problems) or of the regression function (in [[Regression analysis#Regression model|regression]] problems). While the goal of any parametric model is the estimation of a finite number of parameters <math>\theta_1,\dots,\theta_p\in\R</math>, nonparametric models aim to directly estimate the data distribution/regression function.{{sfn|Györfi|Kohler|Krzyzak|Walk|2002|p=9-12}}{{Sfn|Tsybakov|2009|p=1}}

For the mathematical analysis, however, parametric and nonparametric approaches fit into the same setting: Assuming that the function that is to be estimated (data distribution or regression function) belongs to a set of functions parametrized by a set <math>\Theta</math>, one searches for a (measurable) function <math>T_n:\mathcal X^n\to\Theta</math> that estimates the "true" parameter based on data points <math>x_1,\dots,x_n\in\mathcal X</math>. The key difference between parametric and nonparametric approaches is that in the former <math>\Theta\subset\R^d</math> for some <math>d\in\N</math>, while in the latter <math>\Theta</math> is typically the set of possible target functions itself, for example, the set of [[Continuous function|continuous functions]] or [[Differentiable function|differentiable functions]].

Relevant questions in this field regard the construction of reasonable estimators, [[Consistent estimator|consistency]], rates of convergence and their optimality, and adaptive estimation.{{Sfn|Tsybakov|2009|p=vii}}

=== Consistency ===
As in [[parametric statistics]], a desirable property for an estimator <math>\hat{f_n}</math> is that it converges to the target function <math>f</math> as the sample size <math>n</math> goes to infinity, that is, the approximation error converges to zero. Usually, the approximation is measured in terms of <math>L^2</math>-norm distance between <math>\hat{f_n}</math> and <math>f</math>. Since the estimator is a function of the randomly drawn data <math>X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)</math>, the approximation is a random variable as well, and so we distinguish two different modes of convergence:

'''Weak consistency:''' <math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[\lVert \hat{f_n}(X)-f\rVert_{L^2}^2]=0</math>.

'''Strong consistency:''' <math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\lVert \hat{f_n}(X)-f\rVert_{L^2}^2=0</math> [[almost surely]].

If an estimator is consistent for all [[Square-integrable function|square-integrable]] <math>f</math>, then it is called '''universally consistent'''.{{sfn|Györfi|Kohler|Krzyzak|Walk|2002|p=13}}

Many common nonparametric estimators are weakly universally consistent under suitable choice of model hyperparameters, for example, the [[Kernel regression|Nadarya-Watson estimator]], [[K-nearest neighbors algorithm|kNNs]] and certain [[Local regression|local polynomial estimators]].{{Sfn|Györfi|Kohler|Krzyzak|Walk|2002|p=72, 81, 88}}

=== Minimax optimal rates of convergence ===
A central topic in the statistical analysis of nonparametric estimators is their speed of convergence towards the true target function <math>f</math> and whether the speed is optimal, i.e., the convergence is as fast as possible. The most common way to measure the speed of convergence of an estimator is the [[Minimax estimator|minimax]] convergence rate, which considers the expected loss of the estimator in the worst case scenario. Under certain assumptions on the smoothness of <math>f</math>, one can show that there is a minimal convergence rates that no estimator can undercut, and so any estimator achieving this minimal rate is called optimal.

Mathematically speaking, the target function <math>f</math> is assumed to belong to some class of functions <math>\mathcal H</math>, called the ''hypothesis class'', inducing a distribution <math>\mathbb P_f</math> on <math>\mathcal X</math>, and the approximation quality of an estimator <math>\hat{f_n}: \mathcal X^n\to\mathcal H</math> is measured by some function <math>L:\mathcal H\times\mathcal H\to [0,\infty)</math>. The minimax convergence rate of <math>\hat{f_n}</math> is a sequence <math>(\psi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}</math> of real numbers for which it holds<math display="block">\begin{align}
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{\psi_n} \sup_{f\in\mathcal H}\mathbb{E}_f\big[L\big(f,\hat{f_n}(X_1,\dots,X_n)\big)\big] &<\infty, \\
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{\psi_n} \sup_{f\in\mathcal H}\mathbb{E}_f\big[L\big(f,\hat{f_n}(X_1,\dots,X_n)\big)\big] &>0, 
\end{align}</math>where <math>\mathbb{E}_f[\cdot]</math> indicates that the random variables <math>X_1,\dots,X_n</math>, which draw the data points, have distribution <math>\mathbb P_f</math>.

A universal lower bound on estimation for a hypothesis class <math>\mathcal H</math> is a sequence <math>(\psi_n)_{n\in\N}</math> for which it holds<math display="block">\begin{align}
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{\psi_n} \inf_{\hat{\rho_n}}\sup_{f\in\mathcal H}\mathbb E_f\big[L\big(f,\hat \rho_n(X_1,\dots,X_n)\big)\big] &<\infty, \\
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{\psi_n} \inf_{\hat{\rho_n}}\sup_{f\in\mathcal H}\mathbb E_f\big[L\big(f,\hat \rho_n(X_1,\dots,X_n)\big)\big] &>0,
\end{align}</math>where the infima are taken over all possible estimators <math>\hat \rho_n</math> (that is, [[Measurable function|measurable functions]]) based on <math>n</math> observations.

The detailed analysis of nonparametric estimators then separates into the estimation of probability densities and regressions functions.

==== Density estimation ====
The setting of density estimation typically involves a normed space of functions <math>(\mathcal F,\lVert\cdot\rVert)</math>, a subset of density functions <math>\mathcal H = \{f\in\mathcal{F}: f\geq 0, \int_{\mathcal X} f(x)dx=1, \lVert f\rVert\leq 1\}</math> and independent random variables <math>X_1,\dots,X_n\in\mathcal X\subset\R^d</math> distributed according to the measure with density <math>f\in\mathcal H</math>, which generates the data.

Minimax lower bounds are known for different pairs of function classes <math>\mathcal F</math> and comparison metrics <math>L</math>. Common choices for <math>\mathcal F</math> are:

* <math>\mathcal F=C^\alpha(\mathcal X), \alpha>0</math>: The space of <math>\lfloor\alpha\rfloor</math>-times differentiable functions with the highest derivative being <math>(\alpha-\lfloor\alpha\rfloor)</math>-[[Hölder condition|Hölder]]-smooth.
* <math>\mathcal F= H^s(\mathcal X)=W^{s,2}(\mathcal X), s>0</math>: The space of [[Sobolev space#Sobolev spaces with non-integer k|Sobolev-smooth]] functions with square-integrable [[Weak derivative|weak derivatives]].
* <math>\mathcal F= B^s_{p,q}(\mathcal X), s>0, p,q\in(0,\infty]</math>: The space of [[Besov space|Besov-smooth]] functions.

In fact, the Hölder spaces and the Sobolev spaces are special cases of some Besov spaces, namely <math>C^\alpha(\mathcal X)=B^\alpha_{\infty,\infty}(\mathcal X)</math> for <math>\alpha\notin\mathbb{Z}</math> and <math>H^s(\mathcal X)=B^s_{2,2}(\mathcal X)</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Triebel |first=Hans |title=Theory of Function Spaces |publisher=Birkhäuser Verlag |year=1983 |isbn=9783764313814 |series=Monographs in mathematics}}</ref> Thus, it often suffices to derive lower bounds under Besov-smoothness assumptions.

Common choices for <math>L</math> are:

* <math>L(f,g)=(f(x_0)-g(x_0))^2, x_0\in\mathcal X</math>: The pointwise squared error (MSE).
* <math>L(f,g)=\lVert f-g\rVert_{L^2(\mathcal X)}^2</math>: The [[Mean integrated squared error|Mean Integrated Square Error]] (MISE).
* <math>L(f,g)=\lVert f-g\rVert_{L^\infty(\mathcal X)}</math>: The [[Uniform norm|supremum-norm]]-distance.
* <math>L(f,g)=\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}_f\lVert \mathbb{P}_g)</math>: The [[Kullback–Leibler divergence|Kullback-Leibler divergence]] of the distributions induced by <math>f</math> and <math>g</math>.
* <math>L(f,g)=\mathrm{TV}(\mathbb{P}_f,\mathbb{P}_g)</math>: The [[Total variation distance of probability measures|total variation distance]] of the distributions induced by <math>f</math> and <math>g</math>.
* <math>L(f,g)=W_\beta(\mathbb{P}_f, \mathbb{P}_g), \beta\geq 1</math>: The [[Wasserstein metric|Wasserstein-]]<math>\beta</math> distance of the distributions induced by <math>f</math> and <math>g</math>.

By Scheffé's theorem, the total variation distance <math>\mathrm{TV}(\mathbb{P}_f,\mathbb{P}_g)</math> is equivalent to the <math>L^1</math>-distance of <math>f</math> and <math>g</math>.

The lower bound of the MISE is sometimes compared to the [[Cramér–Rao bound]] from parametric statistics, which is a lower bound for the [[Mean squared error|mean-squared error]] of [[Regular estimator|regular]] unbiased estimators of a parameter <math>\theta</math>:<math display="block">\begin{align}
\sup_{\theta\in\Theta} \mathbb{E}&[\lVert\theta - \hat\theta_n\rVert^2] \geq n^{-1} \underbrace{\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathrm{tr}( I(\theta)^{-1})}_{=const.}, \\
\sup_{f\in B_{p,q}^s(\mathcal X)} \mathbb{E}&[\lVert f-\hat{f_n}\rVert^2_{L^2(\mathcal X)}] \geq c n^{-2s/(2s+d)},
\end{align}</math>where <math>I(\theta)</math> is the [[Fisher information]] of the parametric model and <math>c>0</math> is some constant. The nonparametric rate is thus slower than the parametric rate <math>n^{-1}</math>, especially in large dimensions, and approaches the parametric rate as the smoothness of the density tends to infinity.

[[Kernel density estimation|Kernel density estimators]], for instance, achieve the lower bound w.r.t. the MISE under a Sobolev hypothesis class under an appropriate bandwidth choice and is thus minimax optimal.{{Sfn|Tsybakov|2009|p=15}} More recently, also [[Diffusion model|score-based generative models]] have been shown to achieve minimax convergence rates in total variation and in Wasserstein-1 distance for <math>B^s_{p,q}([0,1]^d)</math>-smooth distributions, <math>s>(1/p-1/2)_+</math>, that are bounded away from zero from below.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Oko |first=Kazusato |last2=Akiyama |first2=Shunta |last3=Suzuki |first3=Taiji |date=2023 |title=Diffusion Models are Minimax Optimal Distribution Estimators |url=https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/oko23a.html |journal=Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning |volume=202 |pages=26517-26582 |via=}}</ref>

==== Regression ====
In the [[Regression analysis#Regression model|regression]] setting, the data arises in pairs <math>(X_1,Y_1),\dots,(X_n,Y_n)</math>. Assuming that the data is independent and identically distributed, and <math>\mathbb{E}[|Y_1|]<\infty</math>, one can always write<math display="block">Y_i = f(X_i) + \varepsilon_i,</math>with <math>f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y_1\mid X_1=x]</math> being the ''regression function'' to be estimated and a ''noise'' variable <math>\varepsilon_i</math> fulfilling <math>\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i]=0</math> and <math>\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^2]=\sigma^2>0</math>. Typically, the independent variables <math>X_i</math> are assumed to have values in the unit cube <math>[0,1]^d</math> and to be either deterministic points on a grid (deterministic design) or uniformly distributed (random design). Thus, <math>\mathcal X=[0,1]^d\times\R</math>.

The above setting applies to [[binary classification]] as well. In that case, the observations take only two values, say 0 and 1, such that <math>f(x)=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_{\{Y_1=1\}}\mid X=x] = \mathbb{P}(Y_1=1\mid X=x)</math> and given an estimator <math>\hat{f_n}</math> of <math>f</math>, the classifiers are assumed to have the form <math>C(x)=\mathbb{1}_{[1/2,1]}(\hat{f_n}(x))</math>, that is, they classify a point as 1 if the estimated probability of <math>Y=1</math> is greater than <math>1/2</math> (and 0 otherwise). Indeed, many classification methods are of that form, for example [[logistic regression]], [[linear discriminant analysis]], [[Quadratic classifier#Quadratic discriminant analysis|quadratic discriminant analysis]], and [[K-nearest neighbors algorithm|k-nearest-neighbors]], and [[Support vector machine|support vector machines]].

Then, for the statistical analysis, the hypothesis class is of the form <math>\mathcal H = \{f\in\mathcal{F}: \lVert f\rVert\leq 1\}</math> for some normed space of functions <math>(\mathcal F,\lVert\cdot\rVert)</math> and expectations <math>\mathbb{E}_f</math> are taken with respect to the joint distribution of <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> (or just <math>Y</math> if the <math>X_i</math> are deterministic).

In [[nonparametric regression]], the hypothesis class necessarily requires some strong assumptions on the regression function, otherwise, the minimax lower bound can be arbitrarily slow. For example, if <math>\mathcal F=L^\infty([0,1])</math>, that is, the set of [[Bounded function|bounded functions]], then for any estimator <math>\hat{f_n}</math> and any zero sequence <math>(\psi_n)_{n\in\N}</math>, there exists <math>f\in\mathcal H</math> such that{{sfn|Györfi|Kohler|Krzyzak|Walk|2002|p=32}}

<math display="block">\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb E[\lVert f-\hat{f_n}\rVert_{L^2([0,1])}^2]}{\psi_n}\geq 1.</math>

Thus, common choices for <math>\mathcal F</math> are:
* <math>\mathcal F=C^\alpha([0,1]^d), \alpha>0</math>: The space of <math>\lfloor\alpha\rfloor</math>-times differentiable functions with the highest derivative being <math>(\alpha-\lfloor\alpha\rfloor)</math>-[[Hölder condition|Hölder]]-smooth.
* <math>\mathcal F= W^{k,q}([0,1]^d), k\in\N, q>d</math>: The space of [[Sobolev space#Sobolev spaces with non-integer k|Sobolev-smooth]] functions with <math>L^q</math>-integrable [[Weak derivative|weak derivatives]].

Common choices for <math>L</math> are:

* <math>L(f,g)=(f(x_0)-g(x_0))^2, x_0\in[0,1]^d</math>: The pointwise squared error (MSE).
* <math>L(f,g)=\lVert f-g\rVert_{L^p([0,1]^d)}, p\in[1,\infty)</math>: The <math>p</math>-th norm.
* <math>L(f,g)=\lVert f-g\rVert_{L^\infty([0,1]^d)}</math>: The [[Uniform norm|supremum-norm]]-distance.
Under certain technical assumptions, the following lower bounds are known.

| <math>n^{-\frac{k}{2k+d}}</math><ref name=":3" /> <math>(\sqrt{n}/\sigma\geq 1)</math>
|}
Some [[Local regression|local polynomial estimators]] are minimax optimal w.r.t. the MSE, <math>L^2</math> and <math>L^\infty</math> under <math>\mathcal H=C^\alpha([0,1]^d)</math> for arbitrary <math>\alpha>0</math> when the bandwidth is of order <math>\mathcal O(n^{-\frac{1}{2\alpha+d}})</math>.{{Sfn|Tsybakov|2009|p=40, 44}} [[K-nearest neighbors algorithm|kNNs]] are also minimax optimal w.r.t. the MSE under <math>\mathcal H=C^2([0,1]^d)</math> and w.r.t. <math>L^2</math> under <math>\mathcal H=C^1([0,1]^d)</math> when the number of considered neighbors is of order <math>\mathcal O(n^{\frac{1}{d+4}})</math> and <math>\mathcal O(n^{\frac{1}{d+2}})</math> respectively.{{sfn|Györfi|Kohler|Krzyzak|Walk|2002|pp=93-96}}

=== Adaptivity ===
The choice of the model hyperparameters (e.g. bandwidth for kernel methods or number of neighbors for kNN) needed to achieve the optimal convergence rate typically depend on the smoothness parameter of the unknown target function, which means that, in practice, without an appropriate estimation of the hyperparameters, the methods named above are in fact ''not'' optimal.

Instead, one is interested in methods that achieve the minimax optimal convergence rates not only for one specific smoothness parameter, but across different values. Let the hypothesis class be of the form <math>\mathcal H=\bigcup_{\beta>0}\mathcal H_\beta</math> (for example <math>\mathcal H_\beta=C^\beta([0,1]^d)</math> or <math>\mathcal H_\beta=H^\beta([0,1]^d)</math>) and let <math>\psi_n^\beta</math> be optimal convergence rate in <math>\mathcal H_\beta</math>. Then, a family of estimators <math>(\hat{f_n})_{n\in\N}</math> is called '''adaptive in the minimax sense''', if there exists a constant <math>C(\beta)</math> depending only on <math>\beta</math> such that{{Sfn|Tsybakov|2009|p=180}}

<math display="block">\sup_{f\in{\mathcal H}_\beta}\mathbb{E}[L(\hat{f_n},f)]\leq C(\beta)\psi_n^\beta,\quad \forall\beta>0,\quad\forall n\in\N.</math>

In other words, an adaptive estimator is required to achieve the minimax convergence rate in all hypothesis classes <math>\mathcal H_\beta</math>, but without taking the unknown parameter <math>\beta</math> as argument. Adaptive estimators are often realized by taking estimators that are minimax optimal for a family of hypothesis classes and by estimating the hyperparameters via a higher-level procedure, such as [[Cross-validation (statistics)|cross-validation]], or by complexity penalization.{{Sfn|Györfi|Kohler|Krzyzak|Walk|2002|p=14-15, 26-28}}

==History==
Early nonparametric statistics include the [[median]] (13th century or earlier, use in estimation by [[Edward Wright (mathematician)|Edward Wright]], 1599; see {{slink|Median|History}}) and the [[sign test]] by [[John Arbuthnot]] (1710) in analyzing the [[human sex ratio]] at birth (see {{slink|Sign test|History}}).<ref name="Conover1999">{{Citation
